articles.title: Sebastian Stan knows 'Fjord' is 'divisive.' He wants to talk about it.
articles.summary: Sebastian Stan has seen your "knee-jerk reactions" to "Fjord," about a conservative family under fire. The response is "unfortunately predictable."
articles.body:
Sebastian Stan knows 'Fjord' is 'divisive.' He wants to talk about it.

NEW YORK – Sebastian Stan knows his latest movie is bound to strike a nerve. He likes it that way.

"I'm proud when I'm a part of something that speaks to a timely issue," says " The Apprentice " star, who is following up his Oscar-nominated role as a young Donald Trump with an equally provocative new drama.

Loosely inspired by a true story, " Fjord " (in select theaters Oct. 9, expanding nationwide Oct. 23) follows a devoutly Christian family led by stern Romanian patriarch Mihai (Stan) and his Norwegian wife, Lisbet ( Renate Reinsve ), who works in a nursing home.

When they relocate to Lisbet's hometown, the conservative clan instantly raises eyebrows among their progressive new neighbors – specifically, when the children's teachers discover bruises on their bodies and the kids confess there's occasional physical discipline at home. They are soon taken away by child protective services, sparking a prolonged legal battle.

"Fjord" grapples with cultural clashes and individual freedom, asking at what point it is our responsibility to police others' values and behavior. The Oscar hopeful won Cannes Film Festival's top prize , the Palme d'Or, in May. But it has also sparked debate among critics and social media users , some of whom believe that it props up right-wing ideology with the film's depiction of protesters rushing to Mihai and Lisbet's defense, claiming religious persecution.

"They're not understanding the nuances," says Stan, 44, on a recent visit to USA TODAY's studio. "I find it almost laughable to label it a 'MAGA film' when it's essentially about an immigrant family going to a different country and being torn apart. We could change Norway for the United States, and Romania for Mexico, or any number of places where that's happening."

Despite "these knee-jerk reactions," it's a film "that has to be processed and downloaded," Stan adds. "In America, it's going right to the heart of this divisive issue that we're currently having, and the reason people are writing it off or feel it's a propaganda piece is because we've normalized finger-pointing. This judgmental, dismissive attitude that plays out online is quite dangerous and naïve – but it's unfortunately predictable in today's time."

As a Romanian immigrant, 'Fjord' felt like 'a coming home' for Sebastian Stan

Born in Romania, Stan and his mother moved to Austria when he was 8 after the Romanian Revolution. They eventually settled in upstate New York when he was 12.

Although his family wasn't particularly religious, "I still had exposure to emotionally guarded, stoic, Eastern European male figures," he recalls. As an immigrant, he understood what it means to "feel different, have an accent, try to make new friends, and have that self-awareness that inevitably ends up carrying a slight degree of shame with it."

After working in the U.S. for roughly two decades, "Fjord" felt like "a bit of a coming-home party for me," Stan says. It's written and directed by Romanian filmmaker Cristian Mungiu, and it's the actor's first movie in which he gets to substantially speak his native language.

"I felt very embraced by the Romanian crew," he recalls. "I hung out with them every night; we spoke Romanian every day. Because I left [the country] so early, I felt like I'd been playing catch-up for a very long time. I definitely feel like I've arrived back to some old place that I left."

Scarlett Johansson, Pedro Pascal arrive at New York Film Festival 2026

In making "Fjord," Stan was very intrigued by the prospect of going to "morally ambiguous" places. While prepping for the project, he had extensive conversations with Mungiu and Reinsve about the characters' respective childhoods. They also visited churches and spoke to parents who have been embroiled in similar legal cases.

"This movie deals a lot with history and tradition, and whether it still has value in today's world. And if so, what still works and what doesn't?" Stan says. "In terms of my own upbringing culturally, there was a sense of: Stick to your own lane, stay suspicious and stay guarded. Also, if you got in trouble, you really got in trouble – and maybe that did involve spanking or a slap here and there.

"I was a very accident-prone kid and I scared my mom," he adds. "I could see she had the right intentions to protect me."

Sebastian Stan says the movie is 'very relevant for me' as a new dad

Stan and his partner, actress Annabelle Wallis, welcomed their first child in July. As a result, "this idea of what we are passing onto our kids is very relevant for me at this time in my life," he says. "It's a movie about: How do you raise kids in today's world? I've been thinking a lot about the things I learned that I'm inevitably passing down."

The Golden Globe winner admittedly has "many" fears about raising a kid in 2026.

"All you have to do is just look at the news, and how we're treating our planet and ourselves," Stan says. "But on a personal level, you always have to look at what you have control over. Even though, as a parent, I have the best intentions for my kid, it doesn't necessarily mean that I am somehow free of fault or making a mistake. It's very easy to impose your own perspective, and not see your child for who she or he or they may naturally exist to be.

"Suppression is a major issue," he adds. "Any time something is suppressed or denied, it grows another head in some capacity."

Since 2011, Stan has been in nearly a dozen Marvel projects as Bucky Barnes, aka the Winter Soldier, and he will appear in an undisclosed role in Matt Reeves' upcoming " The Batman: Part II ." But he has also stretched himself in audacious independent fare including " A Different Man ," "Fresh" and "I, Tonya."

"I like Sebastian when he has to play something very different to what he does in the Marvel movies," says Mungiu, praising the mix of menace and warmth that Stan brings to Mihai. "He is very versatile and capable of expressing a lot by doing very little."

Stan fell in love with acting in high school, and "I never thought I was going to end up in this one role that I was going to be defined by," he says. "I'm always indebted to Marvel because it opened these doors, but I feel like I'm getting to do now what I always wanted to do when I was younger. We're all so overexposed now that it's easy to get comfortable – and I worry about getting too comfortable."

articles.title: Jessica Chastain's horror movie 'Other Mommy' is filled with jump scares. But is it actually scary?
articles.summary: Some critics say the film's nonstop attempts to frighten audiences ultimately have the opposite effect.
articles.body:
As Halloween draws closer , Jessica Chastain's new horror movie Other Mommy is promising plenty of frights.

The supernatural horror film stars Chastain as both a mother and the sinister entity that her young daughter begins to see around their home.

Savage, whose previous work includes Host and The Boogeyman , has said the movie is packed with jump scares and scary moments. He told Empire , "Once it starts, it never stops... It disrupts all of the usual horror beats and rhythms that you associate with the genre. It's got some of the most scary, jump-filled scenes that I've ever shot."

Audiences got an early taste of that over the summer, when the Other Mommy trailer played before screenings of Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey . One scene, in which Chastain's character suddenly contorts into a spider-like creature, caught moviegoers off guard, with some saying the jump scare had terrified them .

But can Other Mommy sustain that panic for an entire movie? Here's what film critics have said.

🎭 Cast: Jessica Chastain, Arabella Olivia Clark, Jay Duplass

Other Mommy follows Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark), a young girl who begins seeing a sinister version of her mother, Ursula (Chastain), around their home. The mysterious entity, which Bela calls "Other Mommy," initially appears friendly but soon reveals a more frightening side.

The movie is based on Josh Malerman's 2024 novel Incidents Around the House .

Do the jump scares in 'Other Mommy' actually work?

Many critics found the relentless shocks in Other Mommy more exhausting than frightening.

Yahoo 's Brett Arnold suggested the movie "gives away its biggest jump scare in the marketing, and it never really matches that pure shock energy again," while the Guardian 's Benjamin Lee called the film "a rickety fairground ride filled with loud jolts and skin-tearing gore."

Variety 's Siddhant Adlakha described an "endless litany of numbing jump scares that grow quickly stale," with many following the same pattern: the camera circles a character before revealing Chastain's demonic double lurking behind them.

"The effort at trying to make this work a hundred different ways would be adorable if it weren't so grating," he added.

Adlakha also argued that genuine threats and false alarms are given "the same weight and energy," making it difficult for the film to build suspense. "Tension dissipates no matter who or what jumps out from darkened spaces," he wrote.

Similarly, Josh Bate of ScreenRant argued that "audiences would be forgiven if most of these scares breezed right by without them noticing. They simply don't land at all. Nothing is scary about Other Mommy, and only the film's very first sequence is even slightly creepy."

Carlos Morales of IGN acknowledged that Other Mommy has "a few effective jump scares," but said there were "nowhere as many" as he expected.

Slashfilm critic Chris Evangelista said the movie "unleashes plenty of ghoulish jump scares," adding that Chastain's fans "will no doubt get a kick out of watching her crawl around on the floor covered in monster makeup while using a creepy voice."

Is 'Other Mommy' scary between the jump scares?

For all its jump scares, Other Mommy has a potentially more frightening idea at its heart: a child who can no longer be sure which version of her mother is real.

Yet Richard Lawson of the Hollywood Reporter found the film "only occasionally spooky," saying it was "missing a sense of dreadful build-up that might help its scares sink in deeper." He called it a "mostly vacuous collection of jumpy bits and half-baked mythology."

Lawson suggested the film could have been more unsettling had it stayed closer to Bela's perspective. He applauded Chastain's portrayal of her emotionally distant mother as a "quietly unreliable and unknowable presence" in the child's life.

ScreenRant's Bate criticized the lack of mystery, arguing that the film reveals too much about its supernatural threat too soon. "The audience immediately has all the answers to the film's story, even before they've met a single character," he wrote, adding that it misses out on the "rising tension" that could have made the story more frightening.

Slashfilm's Evangelista enjoyed some of Savage's visual flourishes but argued that "the creature work is never convincing or distinct enough to be scary."

IGN's Morales was similarly unimpressed, saying the film "doesn't come close to being as unnerving as it clearly wants to be." He criticized its unconvincing CGI effects but praised a brief moment of practical body horror as "agreeably gooey."

Yahoo's Arnold said Other Mommy was "all over the place," but he commended it for "taking some bold swings," while the Guardian's Lee said the "psychological chaos" inflicted by the entity was "far scarier" than the movie's visual effects.

Nick Schager of the Daily Beast was more enthusiastic, praising Chastain's "deliciously devious" performance and the film's "roaring, rampaging craziness."

Though he found the movie "far too superficial and insubstantial to be remembered as a frightening classic," he still called it a "thriller fit for a Friday night out at the multiplex with friends."

articles.title: Escola Almirante Soares Dutra vence o Festival de Bandas de Santarém 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Banda Musical da escola conquistou o primeiro lugar com 318,7 pontos; na categoria Infantojuvenil, a campeã foi a Escola Municipal Maria da Conceição Figueira.
articles.summary: Banda Musical da escola conquistou o primeiro lugar com 318,7 pontos; na categoria Infantojuvenil, a campeã foi a Escola Municipal Maria da Conceição Figueira.
articles.body:
Estudantes realizam apresentação com instrumentos de percussão durante o Festival de Bandas de Santarém na Esplanada Tapajós — Foto: Reprodução/TV Tapajós

A Escola Estadual Almirante Soares Dutra conquistou o título de campeã na categoria Banda Musical do Festival de Bandas de Santarém 2026. O resultado foi divulgado na tarde deste sábado (10), após a apuração oficial das notas, em Santarém, no oeste do Pará. A escola somou 318,7 pontos e ficou à frente das outras concorrentes em uma disputa definida pela avaliação dos jurados.

A apresentação da Almirante Soares Dutra homenageou o maestro Júlio Heleno, reconhecido pelo trabalho no ensino musical de jovens estudantes da região.

O segundo lugar ficou com o Ponto de Cultura Coletivo Banda Musical Frei Ambrósio, que alcançou 316,8 pontos. A Escola Estadual Álvaro Adolfo da Silveira completou o pódio, com 316,2 pontos.

Escola municipal vence na categoria Infantojuvenil

Na categoria Banda de Percussão Infantojuvenil, a campeã foi a Escola Municipal Maria da Conceição Figueira, que obteve 256,2 pontos.

A Escola Municipal Princesa Izabel ficou em segundo lugar, com 251,6 pontos. Já o Centro de Artes Professora Josefa Borges, de Belterra, conquistou a terceira colocação, com 250,4 pontos.

As escolas classificadas em primeiro, segundo e terceiro lugares nas categorias premiadas dividiram R$ 150 mil em premiações, conforme a organização do festival.

O resultado consolidado e as notas atribuídas pelos jurados em cada quesito estão disponíveis no canal oficial da Prefeitura de Santarém no YouTube.

articles.title: Matthew Lillard recalls thinking post-“Scream” night shoot that movie was ‘lame’ and he’d become a TV star
articles.summary: Around this time, he filmed a pilot that never aired.
articles.body:
Matthew Lillard thought that Scream would be a flop.

While filming the horror flick, he recalled thinking that the movie was "lame" and that he'd make it big on television instead.

The TV pilot he filmed around this time never made it to air.

The Scream star explained at New York Comic Con that he didn't have very high hopes for the project when he was making it.

"I was in the back of a car, driving home from work one night, at like six in the morning covered in blood," Lillard said . "I'd been laying in the back of a van, and there's like six actors in the car, and everyone's talking about what they're doing next. And Courteney [Cox] is going back to Friends , and Neve [Campbell] is going back to Party of Five . And I'd literally just been on a pilot, and I'm like, 'This movie's lame. Nobody's gonna see it. I'm going to go become a television star.'"

"That pilot never went, and here we are 30 years later," Lillard said.

He added that "nobody could have possibly ever imagined" what happened when the movie was released, and he has a point. Scream has spawned an entire franchise since its debut, with its seventh installment releasing earlier this year .

Lillard began his career in the '90s, with movies such as Serial Mom , Hackers , and Mad Love . But Scream , in which he played Stu Macher, was his breakout. He's made appearances in some — but not all, because of the way his story arc plays out — of the movies.

Aside from his important role in horror, Lillard has found a place in the Scooby-Doo universe as well, playing Shaggy in live-action and cartoon versions of the mystery series.

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter .

And even with that franchise, Lillard had mixed feelings. He recently confessed that he resented the Scooby-Doo films for years because his role in the live-action films coincided with a career dip.

"It was right about this time, after the second movie, that my career took a real nosedive for a long time," he told Variety in an interview published on Thursday. "Like, I may be one of those guys from the '90s that never comes back. This movie is a love-hate relationship for me because I was like, 'It's Scooby Doo 's fault. That's why I'm not working.'"

While he held some negative feelings about the films for years, Lillard was still glad to have been a part of the franchise.

"I resented Scooby-Doo for a long time," he said. "But I never regretted doing it because the reality is that if I didn't have the money I made in the second film, I wouldn't have made it through."

articles.title: Jessica Biel and Justin Timberlake’s son disapproved of her revealing outfit in ‘Matchbox: The Movie’: ‘Yuck’
articles.summary: The 11-year-old was “very concerned” about one of his mom’s looks in the new Apple TV film.
articles.body:
Jessica Biel shared that her 11-year-old son Silas was not happy with one of her looks in Matchbox: The Movie.

Silas was grossed out by a plunging green dress that his mother wore in the film.

Silas makes a small cameo in the action movie, which premiered on Friday.

Jessica Biel revealed that her oldest son did not approve of one particular look.

In her new film Matchbox: The Movie , which premiered Friday on Apple TV, Biel wears a plunging emerald green dress for one scene, and she revealed that her 11-year-old son Silas was grossed out by the outfit. Biel and husband Justin Timberlake also share a 6-year-old, Phineas.

"My son, Silas, was very concerned about the green dress," she told PEOPLE at the film's world premiere in New York City on Monday. "He was like, 'What are you wearing, Mom? Yuck.'"

Biel confessed she had some anxiety over how her children were seeing her in this completely different light.

"I was like, 'Oh my God, this is intense for them to be seeing this dress,'" she said.

Still, Biel was excited to bring her kids to the Matchbox set and introduce them to their hero John Cena . While her smallest child sometimes struggled to differentiate the pretend world from reality, Silas was excited to get in on the (faux) action.

"He plays a small part in this in the movie at the very end, which is really cute," she told E! News on Monday.

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter .

And as for whether Silas will continue to follow in his mother's footsteps, Biel said that he's currently exploring various creative interests. In fact, he is also tapping into his musical side, taking after his father.

"He's a DJ, so he's kind of interested in both lanes," she continued. "We're just kind of letting him take his time and see what happens and what he really gets interested in."

articles.title: Olivia Culpo and Christian McCaffrey Welcome 2nd Baby, a Boy: ‘Heart Is Exploding’
articles.summary: The couple, who wed in 2024, are also parents to 14-month-old daughter Colette
articles.body:
Olivia Culpo and Christian McCaffrey have welcomed their second baby, a boy

The couple announced on Instagram on Oct. 10 that their son, Roman Augustus, was born on Sept. 29

Culpo and McCaffrey, who wed in 2024, are also parents to 14-month-old daughter Colette

The model, 34, and her husband, Christian McCaffrey , announced in a joint Instagram post shared on Saturday, Oct. 10, that they welcomed their second baby, a boy, on Sept. 29.

"Roman Augustus McCaffrey 🤍," Culpo captioned the post, revealing her newborn's name alongside black-and-white photos of herself in the hospital as she gave birth with her NFL star husband, 30, by her side.

In the photos, the couple, who wed in 2024, could be seen holding their son at the hospital as their 14-month-old daughter, Colette , looked on. Another shot showed Culpo standing in a garden as she held Roman and Colette stood by her side.

"Heart is exploding," the proud mom added in an Instagram Stories post.

Culpo and McCaffrey first announced the news of her second pregnancy on Culpo's 34th birthday in May.

"Best birthday gift ❤️ Baby #2 coming soon 🥹," Culpo captioned a joint Instagram post, which included photos of the pair on a picnic with Colette and their dog, Oliver. A strip of sonogram images was displayed on their picnic blanket.

They later posted a video showing the moment they found out Culpo was pregnant — and how they told their families the happy news.

At the beginning of the video, Culpo and McCaffrey were seen waiting for the results of a pregnancy test.

"You're pregnant!" the San Francisco 49ers running back said before the video cut to them telling their family.

The couple announced their daughter Colette's birth in a joint July 2025 Instagram post , featuring black-and-white photos of themselves with the baby moments after she was born. Shortly after, Culpo shared several color photos from the day on her Instagram Stories as she described childbirth as "the scariest and most rewarding of all experiences."

Last October, Culpo opened up about life at home with her daughter. The new mom shared that she was initially worried that becoming a mom would impact her career.

"There's totally a shift," she said of motherhood during an episode of The Squeeze podcast. "Whether or not you want there to be or not, you have somebody that's physically dependent on you. So I'm not going to sugarcoat it. Yeah, it's scary."

However, Culpo explained that she's been able to lean on her NFL player husband while she's navigated finding a balance between working and motherhood.

"I'm so grateful that I have my husband because while I'm totally working and I'm doing everything in my power to keep working and I'm so happy to have the opportunities that I have," she explained. "Let's say they all went away — would I have the same ability 10, 12, 15, 20 years ago to light that fire up my butt when I have somebody who really needs me, which is my baby? No."

"And I would choose my baby 10 times over, obviously," she added.

articles.title: Tom Zé chega hoje aos 90 anos como o tropicalista desgarrado e inquieto que sempre confunde para explicar | G1
articles.body:
Tom Zé faz 90 anos hoje, domingo, 11 de outubro — Foto: Fernando Laszlo / Divulgação

♬ “Eu tô te explicando / Pra te confundir / Eu tô te confundindo / Pra te esclarecer”, jogou com as palavras Tom Zé em versos do samba “Tô” (1976), composto em parceria com Elton Medeiros (1930 – 2019 )e lançado por Tom há 50 anos no álbum “Estudando o samba” (1976).

Esses versos traduzem o espírito inquieto de Tom Zé e, não por acaso, eles foram apresentados em um dos títulos mais importantes e vanguardistas da discografia deste baiano de Irará (BA) nascido Antônio José Santana Martins em 11 de outubro de 1936, há exatos 90 anos.

Sim, Tom Zé cruza hoje a barreira dos 90 anos como o tropicalista resistente, desgarrado e travesso que sempre confundiu para explicar o que significa de fato ser tropicalista.

Com a alma de um erê , o artista sempre foi uma espécie de Chacrinha (1917 – 1988), o apresentador de TV cujo bordão “Eu vim para confundir e não para explicar” já teve a autoria reivindicada por Tom Zé.

Tom Zé chega aos 90 anos em atividade. Na sexta-feira, 9 de outubro, fez um show comemorativo da efeméride no Circo Voador (RJ), palco de resistência da cidade do Rio de Janeiro (RJ). E vem desenvolvendo um projeto musical para dar continuidade à obra singular e inclassificável que constrói desde a década de 1960.

A trajetória de Tom Zé inclui conexões importantes com os grupos Os Mutantes e Novos Baianos. A ligação com Os Mutantes é notória, até porque Tom Zé é parceiro de Rita Lee (1947 – 2023) em “2001” (1968) – uma das músicas mais famosas do grupo – e em “Qualquer bobagem” (1969), esta também assinada por Arnaldo Baptista e Sérgio Dias.

Já a relação com os Novos Baianos é menos conhecida. Mas o fato é que foi Tom Zé quem, em 1967, apresentou Moraes Moreira (1947 – 2020) – para quem dava aulas de violão – ao poeta Luiz Galvão (1937 – 2022), se tornando o mentor da parceria fundamental que gerou o grupo em 1969, ano em que Tom Zé defendeu a canção “Jeitinho dela” (Tom Zé) com os Novos Baianos no V Festival da Música Popular Brasileira.

Quando ainda estava em Salvador (BA), a trajetória de Tom Zé se entrelaça com as de Caetano Veloso, Gal Costa (1945 – 2022), Gilberto Gil e Maria Bethânia – com os quais fez o histórico show “Nós, por exemplo” em 1964.

Tom Zé é do rebanho tropicalista. Mas logo deixou evidente que seria a ovelha desgarrada. É que Tom Zé nunca fez música para gerar mero sucesso comercial, nunca fez o jogo da indústria. Os jogos armados pelo cantor e compositor no palco ou no estúdio sempre foram puramente estéticos. Tom Zé é e sempre foi um erê que se recusa a entrar na roda-viva do mundo dos adultos sedentos de glória, poder, dinheiro e fama.

Na trajetória mercadologicamente errática, Tom Zé amargou o fracasso comercial de álbuns que somente seriam valorizados anos depois, sobretudo após David Byrne se deparar casualmente em 1986 com o já mencionado álbum “Estudando o samba” e se encantar com a inventividade do disco, compilando a obra de Tom Zé para CD do selo Luaka Bop e, na sequência, lançando pelo selo álbuns inéditos do artista, como “The hips of tradition” (1991) – o que deu prestígio e visibilidade mundial ao último romântico tropicalista.

O encontro de Byrne com Tom Zé em 1988, na cidade de São Paulo (SP), mudou a vida do artista baiano após anos de ostracismo e desânimos com a dificuldade de se fazer ouvir – o que fez Tom Zé cogitar a desistir da carreira e a voltar para a cidade natal de Irará (BA).

Tom Zé, contudo, perseverou e continuou em cena, recebendo as flores em vida. Álbuns gravados após a redescoberta – casos de “Com defeito da fabricação” (1998), “Jogos de armar (Faça você mesmo)” (2000), “Estudando o pagode” (2005), “Estudando a bossa” (2008) e “Tropicália lixo lógico” (2012) – dialogaram com títulos mais antigos como “Tom Zé” (1968), “Tom Zé” (1970), “Tom Zé” (1972), “Todos os olhos” (1973) e “Correio da Estação do Brás” (1978), encorpando discografia pautada pela coerência e pela determinação de inventar.

Aos 90 anos, Tom Zé segue confundindo, mas já não precisa explicar mais nada. Tom Zé é Tom Zé. E isso é tudo. E tudo já está esclarecido.

articles.title: Heidi Klum's fans say she's only making LA 'hotter' after she posts a topless Instagram photo
articles.summary: Heidi Klum turned up the heat with a topless poolside photo in Los Angeles while teasing her bloodiest Halloween costume yet for the 25th anniversary.
articles.body: Heidi Klum is bringing the heat this autumn in a new poolside snap. The 53-year-old supermodel turned up the temperature in a new Instagram photo featuring her lounging poolside, wearing nothing but a small pair of black bikini bottoms. "It’s hot in LA," Klum captioned the post, which shows her lounging topless on a daybed with her dog, with a large grass field and a swimming pool visible behind her. Fans could not help but compliment the German supermodel in the comments section, with one calling her "greatest super model to ever do it" and another saying she is "Absolutely smoking hot." HEIDI KLUM DITCHES BIKINI TOP, COVERS UP WITH POTATO CHIP BAG ON BEACH VACATION A third told her she's "making it hotter" Los Angeles, while another added that the city is "especially" hot "with you there!" Never one to shy away from posting risqué photos with her fans, Klum previously wished her fans a good morning on Instagram with a photo of her standing outside in semi-sheer white underwear and a multicolored shawl with nothing on underneath. articles.body: Amitabh Bachchan once revealed that his immediate thought after securing his debut film was to give his earnings to his parents. During a 2023 episode of 'Kaun Banega Crorepati 15', he spoke about how the opportunity gave him a chance to take care of his parents, Harivansh Rai Bachchan and Teji Bachchan.The conversation took place when contestant Vivek asked Amitabh Bachchan about his first film. Recalling his experience with 'Saat Hindustani', the actor explained that he wanted to use his earnings to bring his parents to live with him. He also spoke about assuming the responsibilities they had carried while raising him.“Humko ye laga ki isase hume jo bhi milega, wo hum apne ma-babuji ko de dein. Mujhe ek zariya mil gaya ki apne ma-babuji ko bula kar apne paas rakhein. Jo zimmedari unhone humare liye jeevan bhar kiya hai us zimmedari ko hum apne kandho par rakh kar aage unke liye kar ke dein.”(“I felt that whatever I earned from this, I should give it to my parents. I had found a way to bring them to live with me. They had taken care of us and fulfilled their responsibilities throughout their lives. I wanted to take those responsibilities onto my own shoulders and take care of them from then on.”)Amitabh Bachchan’s first film and his parentsFor Amitabh Bachchan, the opportunity to act in 'Saat Hindustani' also represented a way to become financially independent and support his family. Rather than focusing only on the prospects of a film career, he remembered thinking about how his first earnings could help his parents.Before entering films, Amitabh Bachchan had been looking for employment in Kolkata. His path towards acting changed after his friend Tinnu Anand recommended him to filmmaker Khwaja Ahmad Abbas. Abbas was looking for new faces for his film 'Saat Hindustani'. According to a 2021 Hindustan Times report, the filmmaker spoke to Harivansh Rai Bachchan before finalising the actor. Khwaja Ahmad Abbas wanted to ensure that Amitabh Bachchan’s father supported his son’s decision to pursue acting.What 'Saat Hindustani' was aboutReleased in 1969, 'Saat Hindustani' followed seven Indian revolutionaries who challenged Portuguese rule in Goa. Amitabh Bachchan portrayed a poet in the film, which marked his debut on the big screen. The project became an important starting point for the actor, who would go on to build a career spanning several decades. His early performance also earned him his first National Film Award in the Most Promising Newcomer category.Over the years, Amitabh Bachchan has continued to work in cinema while maintaining a strong presence on television through 'Kaun Banega Crorepati'. articles.title: Exclusive! Navratri special: Vaani Kapoor: The beauty of Navratri is that we honour the feminine in many forms’
articles.summary: In an exclusive interview, actress Vaani Kapoor reflects on the significance of Navratri, sharing childhood memories and emphasizing the importance of women's empowerment beyond celebrations. Discover her thoughts on the vibrance of Navratri in Mumbai versus Delhi and the importance of connecting across generations.
articles.body: For Vaani Kapoor, Navratri is a celebration of tradition, family and the many facets of feminine strength. Having grown up in Delhi and spent a significant part of her life in Mumbai, the actor has experienced the festival in different ways. In an interaction with Bombay Times, Vaani reflects on her childhood memories of Navratri, the festival’s significance and why women empowerment must go beyond symbolic celebrations.‘Festivals have a lovely way of taking you back to being a child’Talking about her fond memories of the festival, the War actress says, “Growing up in Delhi, I think what I remember most is the vibe during this time of the year. The markets would be buzzing; there’d be Ramleelas happening, and you could feel the excitement building up to Dussehra. At home, I remember the ashtami celebrations, the halwa, puri, and chana, and all the little girls who’d come over for kanjak. As kids, we were more excited about the food and all the festivities than anything else. I think festivals have a lovely way of taking you back to being a child.”‘Mumbai has introduced me to an exuberant side of Navratri’Having experienced Navratri in two cities, Vaani believes each has its own charm. “In Delhi, at least growing up, I remember Navratri being more about the family rituals, the Ramleelas, and the excitement around Dussehra. Mumbai has this wonderful energy during Navratri, with garba, dandiya, music, and everyone coming together to celebrate. Delhi will always feel nostalgic to me because it’s home, whereas Mumbai has introduced me to a different, more exuberant side of Navratri,” she says.‘Empowerment is about the freedom to make your own choices’Navratri is a celebration of the feminine energy in the universe. For Vaani, the festival’s celebration of feminine strength also offers an opportunity to reflect on how women are treated beyond the festivities. “It’s beautiful that we celebrate goddesses and the different forms of feminine strength. But I also feel there’s a difference between celebrating women and truly valuing them in everyday life. So many women grow up being told to adjust, to compromise, to put everyone else’s needs before their own. And we often praise them for how much they can endure, without asking why they should have to endure so much in the first place. Their dreams, happiness, and their individuality matter just as much,” she says.She adds, “I believe that empowerment is about the freedom to make your own choices, to feel safe, to be financially independent, to pursue your ambitions, and to have a say in decisions that affect your own life. These are things every woman deserves, regardless of her background or circumstances. And I think real progress is when women no longer have to fight for things that should be theirs to begin with.”‘There’s something particularly special about seeing women across generations celebrating together’Beyond rituals, music and dressing up, the actress believes festivals create opportunities for women to connect and celebrate themselves. “Festivals have this lovely way of bringing people together, regardless of age or background. And there’s something particularly special about seeing women across generations celebrating together during Navratri, each bringing their own energy to the festivities. So much of our everyday lives revolves around responsibilities that we sometimes forget the importance of just having fun. And I think those moments when you feel part of something where you can simply enjoy yourself, can do more for your confidence than we realise,” she says, adding, “There’s something really comforting about coming together for traditions you’ve grown up with and the memories they bring back. And what I find beautiful about Navratri is that we honour the feminine in so many forms.”Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.summary: AS Roma head to Como on Sunday aiming to reclaim outright first place in Serie A from Inter Milan.Under Gian Piero Gasperini, Roma have made a strong start t...
articles.body:
AS Roma head to Como on Sunday aiming to reclaim outright first place in Serie A from Inter Milan.

Under Gian Piero Gasperini, Roma have made a strong start to their league campaign. They sit at the top of the table with 13 points and are yet to lose in Serie A, combining an attacking return of 14 goals with just three at the other end. Their recent run included four straight victories—4-0 over Fiorentina, 4-0 against Lecce, 2-1 versus Atalanta, and 2-0 away to Torino—before they were held to a competitive 2-2 draw by fellow title contenders Inter Milan.

Roma arrive with several fitness problems following the international break. First-choice goalkeeper Mile Svilar will miss at least a month after suffering a stress fracture in his finger, meaning Pierluigi Gollini is set to deputise in goal.

The midfield is also affected, with Bryan Cristante unavailable because of knee inflammation. That could open the door for Marten de Roon to make his first start, likely alongside Manu Koné.

At the back, Konstantinos Koulierakis is still sidelined, although Evan Ndicka is available and expected to play a key role in the back three.

There is better news in attack, where in-form forward Donyell Malen has recovered from a small knock and should lead the line. Wing-back Wesley França has also been given the all-clear to feature.

However, Gasperini may choose to leave Argentine pair Leonardo Balerdi and Matías Soulé on the substitutes' bench, with their recent international travel likely to be a factor in his selection plans.

Possible AS Roma starting XI: Gollini; Mancini, Ndicka, Hermoso; Molina, Kone, De Roon, Wesley; Dybala, Mora; Malen

The match will kick off at 11:30am BST on Sunday, 10th October.

articles.body: Big B’s b’day: KMC invites its star alumnus backOne may wonder what makes Kirori Mal College’s auditorium so special, but for The Players, KMC’s theatre society, and MUSOC, its music society, it is a place where generations of students learnt about themselves and the world. For some, the auditorium was the college itself. So, when it was left in a dilapidated state for years, the college administration, with the help of its alumni, joined forces to save their home. After multiple meetings and sustained efforts involving celebrated alumni including Amitabh Bachchan, Ali Abbas Zafar, Satish Kaushik, Raj Shekhar, Sargun Mehta, Siddharth, Divyendu, Zeeshan Ayyub and Anant Vidhaat, the auditorium is finally back in shape – ready to be reopened soon.A few days before Amitabh Bachchan’s birthday, a delegation led by Principal Dinesh Khattar met the actor on the sets of Kaun Banega Crorepati. And since no meeting with a KMC alumni is complete without a mention of the auditorium, the meeting saw the principal invite Bachchan to the college next year for the inauguration.‘Mr Bachchan’s support in renovating this auditorium has been immense’Bachchan fondly recalled his KMC days and Frank Thakurdas, the mentor who shaped his early acting career and gives the renovated auditorium its name.During the interaction, the principal formally invited Big B to inaugurate the renovated Frank Thakurdas Memorial Auditorium. “He responded graciously, expressing his willingnessto attend, subject to his professional commitments,” shared Principal Dinesh Khattar with us. “For us, it was a special occasion and from the KM staff and college, we would like to congratulate Mr Bachchan on his birthday today. His support in renovating this auditorium has been immense. For me personally, the reopening of the auditorium will represent not simply the completion of an infrastructure project, but the fulfillment of a cherished dream. Buildings acquire meaning through the lives that unfold within them, and I look forward to seeing the Frank Thakurdas Memorial Auditorium become, once again, the beating heart of Kirori Mal College,” he added.‘The auditorium has been a site of play, work and an exposure to the world’One person who has witnessed the auditorium’s fall, its difficult years and now its revival is Keval Arora. As the former staff advisor of The Players, he remembers how on issue led to another, keeping the auditorium out of use for years. “For generations of members of The Players, and I am no exception, the auditorium has been home. It is a site of playand work, with others and by oneself, an exposure to the world, its people, systems and values, a place of refuge. We are very thankful to our Principal Dinesh Khattar for his unwavering commitment and sustained efforts towards realising this dream,” he told us.Shalini Baxi, Convenor, Culture Council, KMC, and an alumna of the college’s music society, adds, “For me, the occasion was especially meaningful. It was a celebration not merely of a distinguished alumnus, but of the extraordinary cultural legacy of KMC.”Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.body: A superstar’s legacy can inspire celebrations that go far beyond cinema, and Rajinikanth’s devoted fans continue to find unique ways to express their admiration. A special kolu in the Azhagumigu Sri Rajini Temple ahead of Navratri is a tribute to the actor’s incredible journey in Indian cinema. The wide-ranging exhibition includes 230-plus photos and representations of the superstar, highlighting his indelible characters and decades-long career. The annual collaboration proves that Rajinikanth’s popularity is not confined to the cinema halls, turning a customary festival display into a homage to his eternal charm.From 'Apoorva Raagangal' to 'Jailer 2': Rajinikanth fan Karthik creates 230 representationsThe special Navratri kolu, created by Karthik, traces Rajinikanth’s journey from his debut film, Apoorva Raagangal, to his upcoming projects, including 'Jailer 2' and 'Dharman.' According to ANI, Karthik began this tradition three years ago and has continued to expand the display every year. One of this year’s major attractions is a portrait of Rajinikanth drawn on a leaf. Speaking about his devotion, Karthik said he had been a fan of the actor for nearly 40 to 50 years and had collected photographs from the early days of his film career. He described Rajinikanth as his family’s kula deivam (clan deity), explaining that the annual arrangement was a personal expression of their faith and admiration.Special Rajinikanth temple Kolu features handmade portraits and daily pujasCreating the display involves more than collecting photographs. Karthik explained that the pictures are carefully cut out, mounted on foam sheets and fabric, and arranged in different styles to give each year’s kolu a distinctive appearance. The temple also conducts regular pujas, while prasadam is distributed to devotees. Different offerings, including sundal, are prepared each day during the celebrations. articles.title: Exclusive! Ranbir Kapoor: When your day involves a lot of people and a lot of noise, a few minutes alone can feel valuable
articles.summary: Ranbir Kapoor shares insights on the importance of solitude in a busy life, discussing his personal care brand Flux Theory and the transformative power of small rituals like taking a shower.
articles.body: Ranbir Kapoor has played characters who wear their hearts on their sleeves, run away from the ordinary and struggle to make sense of the world around them. From the brooding Jordan in Rockstar to the free-spirited Bunny in Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani, the actor has repeatedly slipped into the skin of men who are constantly negotiating with different sides of themselves. Off screen, however, life comes with its own set of demands — long shooting schedules, the pressure of getting a performance right and the responsibilities that come with being a husband and a father.In the middle of all this, finding a moment to oneself can be a luxury. For Ranbir, it need not involve an elaborate routine or a grand escape. Sometimes, it is as simple as taking a shower without having to rush through it. “After a long shoot, I like having a few minutes when nobody needs anything from me. I’m not particular about making it a ritual, but I enjoy a good fragrance and a little quiet. It helps me leave the workday behind,” he tells us.The appeal, he explains, is less about emerging from the bathroom with a sudden epiphany and more about having the space to slow down. When the day involves being surrounded by people, conversations and constant activity, a few minutes of solitude can offer a welcome breather.“When your day involves a lot of people and a lot of noise, a few minutes alone can feel valuable. I don’t come out of every shower with a big realisation. Usually, it’s much simpler than that: I’ve had a moment to slow down, and I’m ready to give my attention to whatever comes next,” he says.While Ranbir doesn't recall a specific instance of a shower helping him crack a difficult scene, he believes that taking a break from work can help him return to it with a fresh perspective. “I can’t think of a particular scene that I solved by taking a shower! But I do think it helps to get a little distance from the work when you’ve been at it for hours. A short break can clear your head, and sometimes you return to a scene with a different perspective,” he says.It is also an idea that connects with his latest entrepreneurial venture, Flux Theory, a personal-care brand he has co-founded. While the brand's premise revolves around the different versions of ourselves that emerge in different situations, Ranbir says the thinking behind it was to make an everyday activity feel more personal. “I think it’s one of the biggest yet one of the most boring categories. Personal care and shower specifically has been largely about functional products. We really wanted to make it a personal and engaging moment for everyone. Also, the idea behind Flux Theory was really interesting — it’s the belief that you get to play different versions of you. Something which I have done quite a lot in my acting career,” he says.The brand's five archetypes — Sage, Sport, Lover, Dreamer and Rebel — might seem like an extension of the many personalities an actor gets to explore on screen. Can a small everyday ritual influence which version of oneself comes to the fore? Ranbir thinks it can, albeit in a more understated way. “Small rituals can definitely affect how you feel. I wouldn’t say a shower turns you into a completely different person, but it can give you a pause between one part of your day and the next. Sometimes that little shift is enough,” he says.A cold shower, particularly after a long day, gets his vote, while music is unlikely to make it to his bathroom routine. “Usually silence. That’s my quiet time,” he says. And perhaps that is the point. In a life where he is constantly switching between film sets, public appearances and family time, those few minutes offer him something uncomplicated: a chance to switch off before stepping back into the world.Rapid Fire: Ranbir in the Bathroom1. If you could step out of the shower as any one of your iconic film characters, who would it be?Jordan from Rockstar. articles.title: Pier premiere celebrates Cromer film-maker's work
articles.summary: Rupert Harold says the rags to riches film was shot across Europe and Norfolk.
articles.body:
A town has turned out in force to support a 19-year-old film-maker ahead of his new film being released on a major streaming platform.

Rupert Harold from Cromer in Norfolk has made his second feature film and has set his sights on becoming the youngest director to win an Oscar.

His film, Crecista, is a rags to riches story filmed across locations in Norfolk, Lake Como, Milan and Naples and features helicopters, sports cars and a yacht, all within a £2,000 budget. The film will be streamed on Amazon Prime.

He said: "The film was received so well I felt such an overwhelming feeling of support and just a great community feel... I don't think it could have gone better."

The red carpet was rolled out on Cromer Pier on Tuesday for a debut screening of the film ahead of its release on Saturday.

He said: "The premiere was absolutely amazing, we had about 400 people there.

"We had supercars, a Ferrari, a Porsche, Rolls Royce and a Corvette there which was crazy."

Crecista, follows a struggling British man who builds a fortune by illegally selling classified government information.

Harold said Cromer Pier features in the film as does central Norwich.

He added: "We also have Blakeney, we have some of the marshes and various shots in Sheringham and we have Sheringham Little Theatre there as well."

Despite working with a budget of just £2,000, Harold contacted people who were kind enough to let him use helicopters, fancy cars, a yacht club and hotel for filming.

Harold started film-making at eight years old and, after getting in contact with Amazon when he was 15, his first feature film Dengard was released when he was 17.

Harold said he was inspired by films including the 1990 film GoodFellas starring Robert De Niro and directed by Martin Scorsese.

He said: "Film-making is so unique because you are able to transport someone into a world you have created for that set amount of time so I'm super excited to see what people think of the story.

"My ambition has always been to win an Oscar for the youngest director. When I was 17, for my last film I stated that I'm going to win an Oscar at 27."

Off the back of filming across Europe, Harold has big plans to take his third feature film to Montana in the United States.

articles.title: Ian McMillan says social media is helping new poets bypass 'establishment gatekeepers'
articles.summary: Poet Ian McMillan talks Barnlsey, fat rascals and social media ahead of Ilkley Literature Festival.
articles.body:
The 70-year-old will be appearing at Ilkley Literature Festival, alongside authors such as Jacqueline Wilson and Kate Atkinson, swimmer Mark Foster and tennis coach Judy Murray.

McMillan, who publishes a Haiku on BlueSky every day, says he finds social media platforms to be "liberating" for those who want to publish new work.

"I think Instagram poetry is fantastic. It's really liberated people who might have felt a bit nervous about the poetry establishment," he says.

"Social media is great for making people feel confident. And to put something on Instagram, a poem or an image, is to actually publish it, isn't it?

"You don't know who's going to see it. And it is, in a sense, easier than trying to negotiate the gatekeepers who can sometimes be a barrier to get new things published."

McMillan's latest book of poems, Red River Valley, is about family life, everyday surrealism, and the effect of austerity on the village near Barnsley where he's lived all his life.

Born in Darfield in 1956, the writer says his hometown continues to be "endlessly inspiring".

"Every morning I get up at the crack of dawn and I go for my early morning stroll around the village that I've done for years and years.

"I try and test myself out when I get back by writing down five things that I've seen on the same walk every day that I've been walking since I was a child," he says.

"Somebody said to me once, do you maintain a base in Barnsley? I said, yeah, I call it my house, to be honest with you.

"They assume that you live in Surrey. And, every now and then, you come up to your pied-à-terre in Barnsley."

McMillan believes staying in South Yorkshire has given him a "long view" of the town, which has bounced back from the years of austerity in the 2010s.

"Barnsley has reinvented itself and people who have been away from Barnsley come back and see what's happening, particularly in the centre of town, but also in the villages.

"There's such a lot of regeneration, there's such a lot of excitement. Taxi drivers will say things like, 'do you know, they're coming down from that Leeds for a night out in Barnsley'.

"There's lots of excitement and regeneration at the moment and that's got to be a good thing because austerity was a terrible thing, and Barnsley seems to have survived it and is thriving."

For McMillan, Ilkley Literature Festival is a trip down memory lane, after performing there in the 1980s.

"When I was a young man first starting out, I did a thing at the Ilkley Literature Festival Fringe.

"I thought it was going to be like the Edinburgh Festival Fringe and it turned out it was me and three other blokes in an upstairs room in a pub and nobody came, but who cared? We were at the Ilkley Festival.

"I saw all kinds of writers there over the years and what's nice about it is, as we know, it's not in London, so people can get to it very easily."

Another of the bonuses of appearing at Ilkley he says, is a trip to Bettys.

"I might treat myself to a fat rascal in Bettys, but you've got to eat the fat rascal quite a long time before the show, because it will clog up your clack, as Ian McKellen would say."

Ilkley Literature Festival runs until 18 October.

articles.body: Vijay Sethupathi has recalled how director Balaji Tharaneetharan considered other prominent actors for ‘Seethakathi’, despite already having Sethupathi on board. The actor turned the memory into a joke, referring to the filmmaker’s interest in Amitabh Bachchan, Mohanlal, and Kamal Haasan. He shared the anecdote at an event for ‘Baththa’, Balaji Tharaneetharan’s latest directorial venture.Released in theatres on October 1, ‘Baththa’ features Vijay Sethupathi alongside Lijomol Jose. During the event, the actor also discussed his decision to make ‘Seethakathi’ his 25th film and explained why its subject appealed to him.Vijay Sethupathi jokes about Balaji Tharaneetharan’s casting choicesVijay Sethupathi played the lead role in Balaji Tharaneetharan’s 2018 film ‘Seethakathi’. Recalling their conversations during the project, the actor said the director had repeatedly imagined other stars in the role.As quoted by NDTV, Vijay said, "When we were doing Seethakathi, he said, 'It would be nice if Kamal sir did this, it would be nice if Amitabh Bachchan sir did this, it would be nice if Mohanlal sir did this.' I thought, 'Damn, I'm right here next to him.'"The actor followed the anecdote with a humorous comparison involving a street dog and a German Shepherd. He used it to describe how people can favour familiar or celebrated names over someone already close to them."The street dog in our neighbourhood roams around happily and looks cute. Even then, people only like German Shepherds. What to do? It was like that... Hey, someone might misunderstand this. It's nothing like that! What I meant to say was that I was close to him, like a local."Why Vijay Sethupathi Wanted ‘Seethakathi’ as His 25th FilmThe actor also spoke about choosing between ‘96’ and ‘Seethakathi’ when deciding which film would mark his 25th project. Both films came his way around the same time, creating a choice about the milestone."At that time, both 96 and Seethakathi came up. There was a question of which movie to announce as my 25th film," he said. Vijay Sethupathi said he liked ‘96’ and expected it to perform well. However, he wanted ‘Seethakathi’ to mark the occasion because of its approach to art and society. "I really liked 96, without a doubt. I knew that the film would definitely do well. I didn't expect such massive success, but I knew the movie would do well. However, I wanted Seethakathi to be my 25th film. Because this art... I don't even know how to put it. During the time we live, while being part of the crowd, we can also look at society and the changes happening around us from above, like a bird."Actor calls ‘Seethakathi’ role a blessingExplaining his connection with the film, Vijay Sethupathi spoke about art's ability to influence society. He also praised the writing behind the character he was offered. "I think art is the reason behind many changes. There is a character who represents that art. Someone had understood that beautifully and written it. So, for me, when I got that character, I thought of it as a huge blessing. Things like this..."‘Baththa’ Features Lijomol JoseVijay Sethupathi’s latest release, ‘Baththa’, also stars Lijomol Jose in a key role. The Tamil film arrived in cinemas on October 1 and has recorded a rise in collections during its second weekend.According to Sacnilk, ‘Baththa’ earned Rs 2.99 cr net in India on Saturday, October 10. The film recorded the collection across 1,731 shows, registering an 81.2% increase over Friday’s Rs 1.65 cr. With Saturday’s earnings, ‘Baththa’ reached an India net collection of Rs 20.10 cr. articles.title: Cheltenham Literature Festival: Author Matt Haig shares joy of books
articles.summary: Author Matt Haig says books are healing for young people struggling with their mental health.
articles.body:
Books have a "magical way" of reaching you when you need them most - and when you are struggling, they "make you feel understood", an author has said.

The writer of bestselling book The Midnight Library, Matt Haig, was a special guest at the Cheltenham Literature Festival on Saturday.

He said it would be a chance to connect with his fans and hopefully inspire younger readers to experience the joy and healing of reading without the "nonsense snobbery" that society puts on it.

Haig said he had ADHD and struggled with school, and at the time found himself "on the cusp of stopping reading for life" because he thought he was the type of person "that shouldn't be reading".

"Part of the problem is were getting narrower and narrower in our idea of what reading is," he said.

"Picture books, graphic books, audiobooks - reading for joy is when you're reading the right book for you.

"Schools send a message to kids that books are inherently educational. It may actually put people off."

Saturday was World Mental Health Day - a topic Haig said was very important to him.

In the past, he has written about mental health and openly shared his experience of depression while growing up.

"When I was going through a breakdown as a young person, I was back in my childhood bedroom, and I was reading, like, Winnie the Pooh and The House at Pooh Corner, and I think they're among the best mental health books ever written," he said.

"I think there's just something very healing about reading because we're interacting in our own minds, but they don't demand a response, you know? It's not WhatsApp, it's not Instagram."

In pictures: Dairy displays and Prince William

'What terminal cancer has taught me about life'

Haig said books were "magical" and reached you "when you need them most".

"If you're not the most gregarious, outward-going person who's well-connected in their social group, then books are vital. Books can literally be life-saving, they can be a friend," he said.

Haig said he hoped the "nonsense" around books and "snobbery" became something of the past.

"We're all readers - it's about how you get the right texts in front of the right people," Haig added.

Co-chief executive for Cheltenham Festivals, Ali Mawle, said reading for joy was particularly important for young people.

"Finding a story they love can open up new worlds, help them understand themselves and others, and create a lifelong relationship with reading," she said.

"As we mark World Mental Health Day, it feels particularly important to recognise the role that creativity, writing and reading can play in helping young people feel heard, connected and less alone.

"Ultimately, we want every young person to have the chance to find a story – or a way of telling their own story – that works for them."

The Cheltenham Literature Festival runs from 9 to 18 October.

articles.title: Nicolas Cage refuses AI waiver for ‘Spider-Noir’; says he may not work with studio again
articles.summary: Actor Nicolas Cage has criticised Amazon over its alleged use of artificial intelligence, saying he refused to sign a waiver allowing the technology to be
articles.body: Actor Nicolas Cage has criticised Amazon over its alleged use of artificial intelligence, saying he refused to sign a waiver allowing the technology to be used on his series "Spider-Noir" and may not work with the studio again.Cage made the remarks during a panel at New York Comic Con on Saturday, where he also hinted that he would feature in the upcoming fifth season of HBO's crime anthology series "True Detective", reported Variety."Amazon is a very AI-friendly company, to the tune of USD 50 billion invested in OpenAI. I am not an AI-friendly actor, so it's like, connect those dots! I'm not a member of their club. I didn't sign the waiver to let him use AI on 'Spider Noir'. I'm probably not going to be working with that studio again, but that's okay," Cage said."Spider-Noir", based on Marvel's "Spider-Man Noir" comics, features Cage as Ben Reilly, a seasoned private investigator in 1930s New York who is forced to confront his past as the city's only superhero following a personal tragedy. It was released in May on Amazon's streaming service Prime Video.The live-action series was cancelled by the streamer after one season last month despite it receiving 11 Emmy nominations, the highest number among the streamer's programmes that year.Cage, however, said he was keen to explore more television projects and revealed that his next assignment could be the fifth season of "True Detective"."My agent's out there somewhere listening. That's okay that I'm the first to announce that, right?" he quipped."True Detective", created by Nic Pizzolatto, is an anthology crime drama in which each season follows a different investigation and set of characters. The series debuted in 2014 with Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson in the lead roles. Its most recent instalment, "True Detective: Night Country", starred Jodie Foster and Kali Reis and was led by creator-director Issa Lopez.The actor also spoke about his interest in collaborating with emerging Gen Z filmmakers, citing Kane Parsons, who transitioned from YouTube filmmaking to Hollywood with the horror film "Backrooms"."I got to get with these young directors who are Gen Z, and they're going at it their own way, whether it's through the YouTube culture or whatever it is. articles.title: ‘I do not carry the burden of Anupam Kher on my shoulders’: Actor on why he avoids the loneliness of stardom
articles.summary: Anupam Kher says he doesn’t let the weight of stardom rest on his shoulders, because carrying it would only leave him feeling isolated.
articles.body: Anupam Kher says he doesn’t let the weight of stardom rest on his shoulders, because carrying it would only leave him feeling isolated. The actor is back on stage after a few years with ‘Jaane Pehchaane Anjaane,' a play that mixes humor and music to explore loneliness and relationships. Kher and his troupe are on a 45-day tour of the US and Canada, performing in several cities and winning praise from audiences along the way.Anupam Kher says an ivory tower makes loneliness frighteningSpeaking to PTI during a break from a script reading session with director Gajendra Ahire, Anupam made it clear that stardom is not something he lugs around. “I do not carry the burden of Anupam Kher on my shoulders,” he said. Reflecting on his tour of North America, he explained that the star in him would begin to look very isolated if he stayed away from everyday spaces, and added, “Anupam Kher as a star will start looking very lonely if he does not sit in this lobby where there is bread and butter shop, a sushi bar or travelling by buses.” He also pointed out that a life in an ivory tower makes loneliness a scary prospect, but he doesn’t live that way. “If you live in an ivory tower, loneliness is frightening. I don’t. I live a very normal life,” Kher said.The play marks Kher’s first attempt at staging a musical, and audiences in the US responded warmly to it. The veteran actor said that Indians living abroad feel a strong emotional bond with the country, which makes the experience special for them. “People outside India are emotionally attached to India and when they see a story, especially being done by a popular actor on stage, they feel closer to the person and closer to the subject,” he said.Anupam Kher’s four decades of theatreKher said he has been choosing plays that connect with audiences on an emotional level. In a career spanning four decades, he has stayed committed to theatre, appearing in productions like ‘Saalgirah’ with his wife Kirron, ‘Kuch Bhi Ho Sakta Hai’ and ‘Mera Woh Matlab Nahi Tha’ opposite Neena Gupta.“I have done Shakespeare, I have done Bertolt Brecht, I have done stylised plays. But when I am doing plays after leaving the movies, I like to do plays which are easily identifiable by the audience. A father in the audience can watch and sort of say, ‘Oh, this is my story’. So, luckily the response has been the same,” Kher said.‘Jaane Pehchaane Anjaane’ looks at relationships and loneliness within a present-day middle-class neighbourhood, weaving together the stories of a widow, a widower, a young paying guest and a woman dealing with a mid-life separation. Through its characters, the play touches on the experiences of three generations: elders living apart from their children, those in middle age, and the young."The revolution in mobile phones, and internet and everything, has led to a loneliness epidemic. Many countries have announced it as an epidemic, and it’s happening in India also. We have reached a stage where smiles and hugs are replaced by emojis. We have lost, I am not saying it cynically, because we live in a world which is changing, and we have lived, but it has taken away a certain amount of human touch,” he added.Anupam Kher’s play marks Swaroop Sampat’s return to theatre‘Jaane Pehchaane Anjaane’, written and directed by Gajendra Ahire, also brings Swaroop Sampat back to the stage after almost twenty years. articles.title: Horror is big business
articles.summary: The genre has become a tentpole across gaming, film, and television.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on how pervasive horror has become, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback, arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started Resident Evil has been around for 30 years, but the survival horror series is more popular than ever. The most recent game, Resident Evil Requiem, has sold 8 million copies since it launched in February, already making it the 14th best-selling game that Capcom has ever made. At the same time, a reboot of the Resident Evil film series from Weapons director Zach Cregger is on pace to become the top-grossing movie in franchise history. This has had the effect of renewing interest in Resident Evil at large; according to a report from Game File, six different titles in the game series have sold at least 3 million copies so far this year. In an earnings report, Capcom called it “a virtuous cycle in which sales of both new and past titles grow together.” Resident Evil isn’t alone. Rather, it’s indicative of an ongoing trend. Horror was once seen as largely a niche genre, but now, thanks to a combination of factors — including the rise of YouTube and widespread influence of indie games and viral memes — it has steadily grown into a dominant force. Horror tends to be cheaper to produce than other genres, but now it also has sales numbers that compete with the biggest blockbusters. It’s not that there haven’t been major horror success stories before. 2017’s It remains the top-grossing horror flick of all time, and the Resident Evil 2 remake from 2019 has sold almost 20 million copies. But in 2026 the concentration of horror hits, particularly across multiple mediums, has reached a new level, making it clearer than ever that scaring audiences is a big business. How it’s going The most obvious example of this in 2026 is in movies. Obsession and Backrooms — two films helmed by young directors who came up through YouTube — have raked in nearly $1 billion combined at the box office. They out-grossed established franchises like Star Wars and even legendary directors like Steven Spielberg. This despite costing a fraction of what a blockbuster film usually costs; Backrooms was made for an estimated $10 million, while Obsession cost less than $1 million. Before that, Iron Lung, another YouTube-centric horror flick, managed to rake in more than $50 million without the backing of a major studio. Horror movies have always been comparatively cheap to make, but now they’re frequently able to make a huge return on that investment. Meanwhile, in the world of streaming, October has become something of a battleground. This year basically every major service has a tentpole series meant to lure subscribers during spooky season. Amazon just released a remake of Stephen King’s Carrie on Prime Video, helmed by Mike Flanagan, who made his name with a quintet of limited horror series on Netflix between 2018 and 2023, starting with The Haunting of Hill House. With Flanagan now at Amazon, Netflix’s big release this year is Below, a six-episode sea monster thriller starring Josh Hartnett and Stranger Things’ Charlie Heaton. Elsewhere, Peacock has a Friday the 13th prequel called Crystal Lake starring Linda Cardellini as Jason Voorhees’ mom, and AMC Plus is putting out a spooky detective series called Yaga, which features Carrie-Anne Moss and Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams. Not to be excluded, Disney Plus is currently airing the 13th season of American Horror Story. The one name missing from this list is Apple TV, but that’s because the service got a jump on things by releasing the horror / comedy hybrid Widow’s Bay back in April. The show then proceeded to win a record number of Emmys, and it remains a fixture on Apple TV’s most-watched list. While streaming viewership data is much harder to come by than box office data, the sheer fact that every major streaming service is investing in horror-related series, with the backing of some major star power, is an indication of just how important it is. And then there are games. While Resident Evil is the biggest name, there are plenty of other titles and franchises that have been buoyed by the current horror renaissance. Silent Hill has been on a steady run, highlighted by the Scottish spinoff Townfall this year, and the iconic Hellraiser just got its first proper video game adaptation. But it’s not just blockbuster releases. Indie horror games have not only been consistent bestsellers on platforms like Steam, they’ve also been the source material for a number of more moderate theatrical hits, including both Iron Lung and Exit 8. And a lot of that success begins with people watching horror games on Twitch and YouTube; Twitch says that viewers watched 287 million hours of horror content between January and September this year, and that the dedicated “horror” tag saw a 6 percent increase in viewership compared to last year. What happens next With the potential to make a lot of money with very little investment, movie studios are naturally jumping all over the trend. Kane Parsons has reportedly signed up for a Backrooms sequel, Obsession director Curry Barker already has a new film due out next year, and Cregger’s next film has some major star power behind it. Meanwhile, studios are searching for the next Backrooms or Five Nights at Freddy’s anywhere they can. Both A24 and Neon are working on competing movies set in the SCP Foundation universe, a sort of terrifying and expansive fan-made project about a mysterious organization that keeps supernatural and paranormal entities secret, while Warner Bros. has scooped up the rights to internet phenomenon Siren Head. Elsewhere, both Silent Hill and Resident Evil have settled on a near-annual release schedule that shows no signs of slowing down — Capcom says that the ongoing success of Resident Evil led to a new quarterly sales record — nor does the horror fixation of major streaming services. Amazon went so far as to poach Flanagan from Netflix with an exclusive deal, and a struggling Xbox has invested in bringing Hideo Kojima’s horror game OD to consoles. Obviously not all of these projects will be major hits. Not every spooky meme will become a Backrooms-level success. But studios, streamers, and game publishers are taking the genre more seriously now because that potential exists, and they seem more willing to take risks because the upfront costs aren’t as high. This means that, unlike other genres, the possibility remains that even as it explodes in popularity, horror will continue to remain weird and unexpected. After all, the best way to scare folks is to show them something new. By the way * Success in one medium doesn’t necessarily translate. While Silent Hill has become a force in games again, the most recent film has been largely forgotten. * The SCP Foundation has garnered plenty of interest from major film studios, but not without some controversy due to its Creative Commons roots. * Box office success aside, 2026 has also just been a really great year for horror movies with the likes of Send Help, Hokum, and 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple. * Another potential venue for horror: interactive shows. Netflix is exploring the space with Unhinged and an upcoming Conjuring spinoff. Read this * The new iteration of Carrie makes some major changes, and in an interview with Collider Flanagan explains what went into updating the story. * The New Yorker has a great rundown on just how YouTube became the place where new horror auteurs are discovered. * 2026 has made it clear just how closely horror and comedy are related, and few people know that more than Jordan Peele, who discussed it in an old interview with The Guardian.

articles.body:
Roma star Donyell Malen received a straight red card for a reckless challenge during an away game at Como, but protested against the referee and the fourth official, arguing that a foul should have been awarded earlier in the move.

Roma star Malen, the current Serie A top goal-scorer, received a straight red card in the 53rd minute of an away Serie A match at Como.

Malen's red card incident in Como vs. Roma explained

COMO, ITALY – OCTOBER 11: Donyell Malen of AS Roma reacts as he walks off the pitch after being shown a red card during the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Como, Italy. (Photo by Claudio Villa/Getty Images)

The Dutch forward battled Jacobo Ramon for the ball, and the pair pulled each other's shirts. When the ball went away from them, Malen tried to win it back but went in with a clumsy tackle, leaving his leg straight and his studs up.

Referee Michael Fabbri didn't even need VAR intervention; he showed a straight red card within seconds.

DAZN referee expert Luca Marelli commented on the incident live and agreed that the decision was correct: "The red card was the right call. It's true that he got a slight touch on the ball with his foot, but he goes in recklessly with his foot above the ankle, his knee locked, and at speed. In my opinion, it was the correct decision."

COMO, ITALY – OCTOBER 11: Donyell Malen of AS Roma is challenged by Jacobo Ramon of Como 1907 during the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Como, Italy. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

Roma coach Gian Piero Gasperini protested on the touchline, alongside Roma's reserves on the bench.

DAZN pitchside reporter Davide Bernardi said Malen and Roma's players on the sidelines told the fourth official the same thing as the Dutch striker left the field: "It's always foul before."

Malen is convinced his challenge with Ramon should have resulted in a foul in his favour, yet the referee let play continue and then punished the Dutchman for his reckless tackle.

Curiously, referee Fabbri picked up an injury a few minutes later, forcing fourth official Simone Sozza to replace him for the remainder of the game.

articles.title: Nana Patekar’s cause of death revealed: Autopsy report finds blood clot in left main coronary artery
articles.summary: Actor Nana Patekar died of a heart attack caused by a blood clot blocking the left main coronary artery, which supplies blood to a significant portion of
articles.body: Actor Nana Patekar died of a heart attack caused by a blood clot blocking the left main coronary artery, which supplies blood to a significant portion of the heart, according to his postmortem report. A senior doctor at the state-run Goa Medical College and Hospital (GMCH) confirmed the findings on Sunday.According to news agency PTI, the autopsy established the cause of death as “acute myocardial infarction due to left main coronary artery thrombosis secondary to atherosclerotic occlusive coronary artery disease, a natural cause of death”.The 75-year-old actor was rushed to a private hospital in the early hours of October 8 after falling ill at his residence in Dona Paula, near Panaji. His caretaker had contacted the hospital requesting an ambulance, following which one was dispatched to his apartment, located less than a kilometre away.Despite doctors attempting cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for approximately 45 minutes, Patekar could not be revived. He was declared dead at 5.10 am, with a doctor initially suspecting a heart attack. articles.title: Serie A | Como 0-0 Roma: Giallorossi resist under siege after Malen sees red
articles.summary: Roma were ultimately pleased with the first 0-0 of the Serie A season away to Como, as Donyell Malen was sent off for dangerous play, leaving them down to 10...
articles.body:
Roma were ultimately pleased with the first 0-0 of the Serie A season away to Como, as Donyell Malen was sent off for dangerous play, leaving them down to 10 men for over 30 minutes.

These sides snatched Champions League qualification from more prestigious clubs last season and were hoping to repeat it. The hosts lost Moise Kean to injury on international duty and needed to shake off the surprising 2-0 defeat to Frosinone. The Giallorossi lost Mile Svilar for at least a month to a fractured toe, so Pierluigi Gollini got his first Serie A appearance in two years, while Lorenzo Pellegrini replaced injured Bryan Cristante.

ITALY – OCTOBER 11: Cesc Fabregas, Manager of Como 1907, and Gian Piero Gasperini, Manager of AS Roma, embrace before the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Italy. (Photo by Claudio Villa/Getty Images)

Paulo Dybala scuffed a finish straight at Jean Butez after a Donyell Malen knockdown, then Gollini rushed off his line to close down Nico Paz at the near post, but Pellegrini came closest with a strike thumping the base of the upright from the edge of the area on 11 minutes.

Gianluca Mancini's scuffed clearance after an awkward bounce allowed Maxence Caqueret to drill inches wide, then Malen flicked a long Pellegrini ball around Butez, but the angle was too narrow to score.

Gollini made just one appearance last season for Roma in the Europa League, but didn't seem rusty as he rushed out to smother at the feet of Caqueret on a Yan Couto through ball.

ITALY – OCTOBER 11: Wesley of AS Roma is challenged by Assane Diao of Como 1907 during the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Italy. (Photo by Claudio Villa/Getty Images)

On the stroke of half-time, Wesley clipped Assane Diao's heel as he was running towards goal, but the referee waved play on and only booked the Como player for dissent, much to the incredulity of Cesc Fabregas. It was an extremely risky situation, but Evan Ndicka's presence perhaps rescued Wesley from a VAR intervention.

The referee was involved again after the restart, because he flashed a straight red card at Malen. The Roma striker lunged into a tackle after a heavy touch, but went over the ball and studs-up on Bruno Kaiki's ankle. It was clumsy more than malicious, but certainly high, late, and somewhat out of control.

ITALY – OCTOBER 11: Donyell Malen of AS Roma reacts after he receives a red card from referee Michael Fabbri during the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Italy. (Photo by Claudio Villa/Getty Images)

Como nearly took advantage moments later, but Maxi Perrone ballooned over from 12 yards after Diao sent Wesley to ground, then Tasos Douvikas smashed his finish against the side-netting.

There was an odd situation on 67 minutes when referee Michael Fabbri sustained a knee injury, so had to exchange places with fourth official Simone Sozza for the final 20 minutes.

ITALY – OCTOBER 11: Referee Michael Fabbri receives medical treatment during the Serie A match between Como 1907 and AS Roma at Giuseppe Sinigaglia Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Italy. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

Gollini flew to palm a Nico Paz snapshot over the bar from the D, and rushed off his line again to deny the Argentina talent on a ball over the top.

Roma were under siege for the final stages, Mancini throwing himself in the way of a Trevoh Chalobah effort and Douvikas skimming the far post with an angled drive in stoppages.
